svg.title: Routing layer protection: authenticated sessions with a key rotation plan, prefix limits, and the policy that stops leakage
svg.desc: Left: the three phases of a key rotation done without dropping a session. Phase one, the new key is configured alongside the old one on both peers and both are accepted, so sessions stay up. Phase two, the peers are confirmed to be using the new key by looking at the last key id in the neighbour detail output. Phase three, the old key is removed, one peer at a time, with the session verified between each step. Rotating by replacing the key in one step works only if the maintenance window is exactly aligned on both ends - the usual outcome is a session that flaps for a week because someone forgot a peer. Right: the prefix limit ladder for an eBGP session: a warning threshold at eighty percent, a restart threshold at a hundred percent, and a discussion about whether the session should restart at all. A limit that restarts protects the router's memory and takes the customer offline; decide which failure you prefer before configuring it. Bottom: the three layers and what each answers - authentication (is this update from my peer), prefix limits (how much can this peer inject), and policy (which of those prefixes may be used). A footer notes that RPKI origin validation belongs in the third layer: it answers whose prefix it is, not whether the sender is lying about being the peer.
svg.text: Authentication, prefix limits and policy answer three different questions
And a key rotation without a plan is an outage scheduled for the next maintenance window.
KEY ROTATION WITHOUT DROPPING A SESSION
phase 1
new key added beside
the old, both accepted
phase 2
verify both peers send
with the new key id
phase 3
remove the old key,
one peer at a time
Doing it in one step works only if both ends change in the same minute, and someone always forgets a peer.
WHAT EACH LAYER ANSWERS
authentication: "is this update from my configured peer?" - HMAC, SHA preferred over MD5
prefix limit: "how many prefixes may this peer inject?" - binds memory and CPU
policy: "which of those may be used?" - filters, communities, RPKI origin validation
PREFIX LIMIT LADDER
80% warning, log and alert
95% second warning, call the peer
100% restart the session?
restart protects memory and takes the
customer offline - decide which failure
you prefer before configuring it
many operators prefer shutdown over restart:
an idle session you can see beats a flapping one
WHERE RPKI SITS
it answers "whose prefix is this", not
"is the sender who it claims to be"
so it belongs in policy, next to filters,
and it does nothing for a hijack from
the legitimate peer's own AS
THE FAILURES THESE PREVENT
a forged hello or update from a host on the link - authentication
a misconfigured peer announcing the full table - prefix limit
your own prefixes leaking out of an unintended exit - policy, outbound
someone else's prefix accepted as legitimate - RPKI plus filters
Note the direction people forget: outbound policy protects the internet from you, and it is the one a transit provider will ask about first.
Both authentication and prefix limits are per neighbour, which means the review question is: which neighbours still have neither?
Test the rotation plan in a lab once. The first real rotation should not be the test.
